claims.text: A conventional tempered martensitic low-alloy steel can be used to produce a ductile–brittle–ductile transition.
Tempering induces impurity segregation at grain boundaries within a narrow temperature range.
The initial steel is an as-quenched martensitic low-alloy steel.
The initial steel has a homogeneous distribution of low-concentration impurities.
The relevant embrittlement window is typically around 400–500°C.
Phosphorus and sulfur can segregate to grain boundaries during tempering.
Grain-boundary impurity segregation temporarily reduces grain-boundary cohesion.
The temporary reduction in grain-boundary cohesion causes embrittlement.
Outside the narrow embrittlement window, impurity effects are minimized and ductility is recovered.
The steel will have high ductility after tempering at both low and high temperatures.
The steel will exhibit a distinct decrease in ductility at intermediate tempering temperatures.
Low-alloy steel processed without controlled tempering will not exhibit a pronounced ductile–brittle–ductile transition.
The transition is expected only in conventional alloys having simple compositions and controlled impurity levels.
The proposed transition does not apply to compositionally complex or high-entropy alloy systems.
The embrittlement temperature range and the relative contributions of individual impurities may vary with alloy composition and processing conditions.
